content.title: Why Haven’t Astronauts Returned to the Moon in 50 Years? Inside the Technical and Financial Challenges
content.text: NASA Prepares For Artemis II Moon Mission on March 30, 2026 in Cape Canaveral, Florida; Eugene Cernan using the Rover on the lunar surface in December 1972. Credit : Bill Ingalls/NASA/Getty; Heritage Space/Heritage Images/Getty NEED TO KNOW Astronauts haven't landed on the moon since 1972, and NASA has delayed another lunar landing until 2028Outdated Apollo-era technology and lost expertise have made modern moon landings more difficultIn addition, NASA’s budget has dropped from over 4% of federal spending during Apollo to about 0.4% today Technology has advanced astronomically in the 53 years since Apollo 17. But returning humans to the moon is more complicated than ever. Lunar exploration slowed after the Space Race missions of the 1960s and 1970s, as NASA shifted its focus to low-Earth orbit, developing the Space Shuttle program and later helping build the International Space Station. Global interest renewed in 2019 when China's Chang'e-4 probe landed on the far side of the moon, as private spaceflight efforts from companies like Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin and Elon Musk's SpaceX also gained momentum. Though no astronauts — including the four aboard the 2026 Artemis II mission — have landed on the moon since 1972, bold predictions about humanity’s future there have continued. One NASA official declared in 2022 that people would be living on the moon within a decade, and the agency has since outlined plans for a $20-billion lunar base as part of its goal to return astronauts to the surface by 2028. So why haven’t astronauts returned to the moon in more than 50 years? Here’s everything to know about the technical challenges and financial constraints behind the delay. It’s been over 50 years since astronauts walked on the moon Astronaut John Young on the lunar surface during the Apollo 16 mission on April 21, 1972. Heritage Space/Heritage Images/Getty NASA astronauts have been to the moon six times, the last of which was Apollo 17 on Dec. 19, 1972. Congress had already cut NASA's budget before the mission, canceling planned follow-ups and shifting the focus toward the Space Shuttle. As public interest declined, so did support for lunar exploration. “Because it was the first time, there was an energy," Charlie Mars, who worked on Apollo’s command and lunar modules, told the Associated Press in March 2026. "There was a passion that probably is not exactly the same today and hasn’t been for a while.” Much of the technology used in Apollo is now outdated NASA's 322-foot-tall Artemis II Space Launch System rocket and Orion spacecraft at Kennedy Space Center on March 31, 2026 in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Because it’s been decades since astronauts last landed on the moon, the technology used during Apollo is too outdated to rely on. Many of the experts who built and operated those systems are no longer in the field, resulting in the loss of "a lot of that knowledge," according to John Thornton, CEO of Pittsburgh-based Astrobotic Technology. "That whole generation is out of the industry at this point," he told Live Science in March 2024. "We are relearning how to do this, but we're also learning it with technology that is new and different." Multiple technical challenges in this new era of lunar exploration have delayed a return to the moon. These include developing next-generation spacesuits, addressing issues with NASA's spaceraft Orion's heat shield and building a new lunar landing system, per Space.com. NASA no longer has the same budget or structure as Apollo Eugene A. Cernan on the lunar surface during NASA's final lunar landing mission in 1972. Heritage Space/Heritage Images via Getty Landing on the moon is, understandably, expensive. When Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin and Neil Armstrong planted the American flag on its surface in 1969, NASA’s budget accounted for more than 4% of federal spending, per The Washington Post. By 2025, TIME reported that NASA’s share had dwindled down to 0.4%. Related Stories To help offset limited funding, NASA has turned to private companies to build key components for its lunar missions. But that approach can come with growing pains. Dr. Joshua Rasera, a research associate at Imperial College London, told The Guardian in January 2024 that many of these groups are effectively “doing these missions on pocket change,” which can lead to early failures. “It still ends up being cheaper over the total number of missions,” he added, “even if the first few maybe crash.” A mission to land on the moon could launch as soon as 2028 Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin unfurl the US flag on the moon in 1969. Oxford Science Archive/Print Collector/Getty Though Artemis II was not designed for a lunar landing, NASA still has its sights set on returning astronauts to the moon before the end of the decade. In February 2026, officials announced that Artemis IV is expected to mark the program’s first landing as early as 2028 with a potential second landing that same year, per Space.com. These missions are part of NASA’s broader effort to establish a long-term presence on the moon over the next decade. Announced in March 2026, the plan shifts focus away from the agency’s previously proposed lunar-orbiting Gateway station, with some materials expected to be repurposed for future surface infrastructure. “NASA is committed to achieving the near‑impossible once again, to return to the Moon before the end of President Trump’s term, build a Moon base, establish an enduring presence, and do the other things needed to ensure American leadership in space," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a press release.
